The Secure Shell (SSH)\n    28→Protocol is a protocol for secure remote login and other secure network services\n    29→over an insecure network. See [ssh](ssh_app.md#supported) for details of\n    30→supported RFCs, versions, algorithms and unicode handling.\n    31→\n    32→With the SSH application it is possible to start _clients_ and to start\n    33→_daemons_ (servers).\n    34→\n    35→Clients are started with `connect/2`, `connect/3` or `connect/4`. They open an\n    36→encrypted connection on top of TCP/IP. In that encrypted connection one or more\n    37→channels could be opened with\n    38→[ssh_connection:session_channel/2,4](`ssh_connection:session_channel/2`).\n    39→\n    40→Each channel is an isolated \"pipe\" between a client-side process and a\n    41→server-side process. Those process pairs could handle for example file transfers\n    42→(sftp) or remote command execution (shell, exec and/or cli). If a custom shell\n    43→is implemented, the user of the client could execute the special commands\n    44→remotely. Note that the user is not necessarily a human but probably a system\n    45→interfacing the SSH app.\n    46→\n    47→A server-side subssystem (channel) server is requested by the client with\n    48→`ssh_connection:subsystem/4`.\n    49→\n    50→A server (daemon) is started with [daemon/1](`daemon/2`), `daemon/2` or\n    51→[daemon/3](`daemon/2`). Possible channel handlers (subsystems) are declared with\n    52→the [subsystem](`t:subsystem_daemon_option/0`) option when the daemon is\n    53→started.\n    54→\n    55→To just run a shell on a remote machine, there are functions that bundles the\n    56→needed three steps needed into one: [shell/1,2,3](`shell/1`). Similarly, to just\n    57→open an sftp (file transfer) connection to a remote machine, the simplest way is\n    58→to use [ssh_sftp:start_channel/1,2,3](`ssh_sftp:start_channel/1`).\n    59→\n    60→To write your own client channel handler, use the behaviour\n    61→`m:ssh_client_channel`. For server channel handlers use `m:ssh_server_channel`\n    62→behaviour (replaces ssh_daemon_channel).\n    63→\n    64→Both clients and daemons accept options that control the exact behaviour. Some\n    65→options are common to both. The three sets are called\n    66→[Client Options](`t:client_options/0`), [Daemon Options](`t:daemon_options/0`)\n    67→and [Common Options](`t:common_options/0`).\n    68→\n    69→The descriptions of the options uses the\n    70→[Erlang Type Language](`e:system:typespec.md`) with explaining text.\n    71→\n    72→> #### Note {: .info }\n    73→>\n    74→> See also [SSH Application Reference](index.html) and [Examples](using_ssh.md) section.\n    75→\n    76→## Keys and files\n    77→\n    78→A number of objects must be present for the SSH application to work. Those\n    79→objects are per default stored in files. The default names, paths and file\n    80→formats are the same as for [OpenSSH](http://www.openssh.com). Keys could be\n    81→generated with the `ssh-keygen` program from OpenSSH. See the\n    82→[User's Guide](using_ssh.md#running-an-erlang-ssh-daemon).\n    83→\n    84→The paths could easily be changed by options:\n    85→[`user_dir`](`t:ssh_file:user_dir_common_option/0`) and\n    86→[`system_dir`](`t:ssh_file:system_dir_daemon_option/0`).\n    87→\n    88→A completely different storage could be interfaced by writing callback modules\n    89→using the behaviours `m:ssh_client_key_api` and/or `m:ssh_server_key_api`. A\n    90→callback module is installed with the option\n    91→[`key_cb`](`t:key_cb_common_option/0`) to the client and/or the daemon.\n    92→\n    93→### Daemons\n    94→\n    95→The keys are by default stored in files:\n    96→\n    97→- Mandatory: one or more _Host key(s)_, both private and public. The\n   270→modifications are applied after the option `preferred_algorithms` (if existing)\n   271→is applied.\n   272→\n   273→The algorithm for modifications works like this:\n   274→\n   275→- Input is the `t:modify_algs_list/0` and a set of algorithms `A` obtained from\n   276→  the `preferred_algorithms` option if existing, or else from the\n   277→  [ssh:default_algorithms/0](`default_algorithms/0`).\n   278→- The head of the `t:modify_algs_list/0` modifies `A` giving the result `A'`.\n   279→\n   280→  The possible modifications are:\n   281→\n   282→  - Append or prepend supported but not enabled algorithm(s) to the list of\n   283→    algorithms. If the wanted algorithms already are in `A` they will first be\n   284→    removed and then appended or prepended,\n   285→  - Remove (rm) one or more algorithms from `A`.\n   286→\n   287→- Repeat the modification step with the tail of `t:modify_algs_list/0` and the\n   288→  resulting `A'`.\n   289→\n   290→If an unsupported algorithm is in the `t:modify_algs_list/0`, it will be\n   291→silently ignored\n   292→\n   293→If there are more than one modify_algorithms options, the result is undefined.\n   294→\n   295→Here is an example of this option:\n   296→\n   297→```text\n   298→\t  {modify_algorithms,\n   299→\t  [{prepend, [{kex, ['diffie-hellman-group1-sha1']}],\n   300→\t  {rm,      [{compression, [none]}]}\n   301→\t  ]\n   302→\t  }\n   303→```\n   304→\n   305→The example specifies that:\n   306→\n   307→- the old key exchange algorithm 'diffie-hellman-group1-sha1' should be the main\n   308→  alternative. It will be the main alternative since it is prepened to the list\n   309→- The compression algorithm none (= no compression) is removed so compression is\n   310→  enforced\n   311→\n   312→For background and more examples see the\n   313→[User's Guide](configure_algos.md#introduction).\n   314→\"\"\".\n   315→-doc(#{title => <<\"Common Options\">>}).\n   316→-type modify_algs_list()      :: list( {append,algs_list()} | {prepend,algs_list()} | {rm,algs_list()} ) .\n   317→\n   318→-type internal_options()      :: ssh_options:private_options().\n   319→-type socket_options()        :: [gen_tcp:connect_option() | gen_tcp:listen_option()].\n   320→\n   321→-doc(#{title => <<\"Client Options\">>}).\n   322→-type client_options()        :: [ client_option() ] .\n   323→-doc(#{title => <<\"Daemon Options\">>}).\n   324→-type daemon_options()        :: [ daemon_option() ].\n   325→\n   326→-doc(#{title => <<\"Common Options\">>}).\n   327→-type common_options() :: [ common_option() ].\n   328→-doc \"\"\"\n   329→The options above can be used both in clients and in daemons (servers). The term\n   762→in the return value is formatted to a string if it is a non-string type. No\n   763→trailing newline is added in the ok-case.\n   764→\n   765→See the User's Guide section on\n   766→[One-Time Execution](using_ssh.md#one-time-execution) for examples.\n   767→\n   768→Error texts are returned on channel-type 1 which usually is piped to `stderr` on\n   769→e.g Linux systems. Texts from a successful execution are returned on\n   770→channel-type 0 and will in similar manner be piped to `stdout`. The exit-status\n   771→code is set to 0 for success and 255 for errors. The exact results presented on\n   772→the client side depends on the client and the client's operating system.\n   773→\n   774→In case of the `{direct, exec_fun()}` variant or no exec-option at all, all\n   775→reads from `standard_input` will be from the received data-events of type 0.\n   776→Those are sent by the client. Similarly all writes to `standard_output` will be\n   777→sent as data-events to the client. An OS shell client like the command 'ssh'\n   778→will usually use stdin and stdout for the user interface.\n   779→\n   780→The option cooperates with the daemon-option\n   781→[`shell`](`t:shell_daemon_option/0`) in the following way:\n   782→\n   783→- **1\\. If neither the [`exec-option`](`t:exec_daemon_option/0`) nor the\n   784→  [`shell-option`](`t:shell_daemon_option/0`) is present:** - The default Erlang\n   785→  evaluator is used both for exec and shell requests. The result is returned to\n   786→  the client.\n   787→\n   788→- **2\\. If the [`exec_spec`](`t:exec_daemon_option/0`)'s value is `disabled`\n   789→  (the [`shell-option`](`t:shell_daemon_option/0`) may or may not be\n   790→  present):** - No exec-requests are executed but shell-requests are not\n   791→  affected, they follow the [`shell_spec`](`t:shell_daemon_option/0`)'s value.\n   792→\n   793→- **3\\. If the [`exec-option`](`t:exec_daemon_option/0`) is present and the\n   794→  [`exec_spec`](`t:exec_daemon_option/0`) value =/= `disabled` (the\n   795→  [`shell-option`](`t:shell_daemon_option/0`) may or may not be present):** -\n   796→  The [`exec_spec`](`t:exec_daemon_option/0`) `fun()` is called with the same\n   797→  number of parameters as the arity of the fun, and the result is returned to\n   798→  the client. Shell-requests are not affected, they follow the\n   799→  [`shell_spec`](`t:shell_daemon_option/0`)'s value.\n   800→\n   801→- **4\\. If the [`exec-option`](`t:exec_daemon_option/0`) is absent, and the\n   802→  [`shell-option`](`t:shell_daemon_option/0`) is present with the default Erlang\n   803→  shell as the [`shell_spec`](`t:shell_daemon_option/0`)'s value:** - The\n   804→  default Erlang evaluator is used both for exec and shell requests. The result\n   805→  is returned to the client.\n   806→\n   807→- **5\\. If the [`exec-option`](`t:exec_daemon_option/0`) is absent, and the\n   808→  [`shell-option`](`t:shell_daemon_option/0`) is present with a value that is\n   809→  neither the default Erlang shell nor the value `disabled`:** - The\n   810→  exec-request is not evaluated and an error message is returned to the client.\n   811→  Shell-requests are executed according to the value of the\n   812→  [`shell_spec`](`t:shell_daemon_option/0`).\n   813→\n   814→- **6\\. If the [`exec-option`](`t:exec_daemon_option/0`) is absent, and the\n   815→  [`shell_spec`](`t:shell_daemon_option/0`)'s value is `disabled`:** - Exec\n   816→  requests are executed by the default shell, but shell-requests are not\n   817→  executed.\n   818→\n   819→If a custom CLI is installed (see the option\n   820→[`ssh_cli`](`t:ssh_cli_daemon_option/0`)) the rules above are replaced by thoose\n   821→implied by the custom CLI.\n   822→\n   823→> #### Note {: .info }\n   824→>\n   825→> The [`exec-option`](`t:exec_daemon_option/0`) has existed for a long time but\n   826→> has not previously been documented. It is disabled by default.\n   931→\n   932→  The term \"user\" is used differently in OpenSSH and SSH in Erlang/OTP: see more\n   933→  in the [User's Guide](terminology.md#the-term-user).\n   934→\n   935→  If the option is enabled, and no [`pwdfun`](`m:ssh#option-pwdfun`) is present,\n   936→  the user name must present in the\n   937→  [user_passwords](`m:ssh#option-user_passwords`) for the check to succeed but\n   938→  the value of the password is not checked.\n   939→\n   940→  In case of a [`pwdfun`](`m:ssh#option-pwdfun`) checking the user, the atom\n   941→  `pubkey` is put in the password argument.\n   942→\n   943→- **`password`{: #option-password }** - Provides a global password that\n   944→  authenticates any user.\n   945→\n   946→  > #### Warning {: .warning }\n   947→  >\n   948→  > Intended to facilitate testing.\n   949→  >\n   950→  > From a security perspective this option makes the server very vulnerable.\n   951→\n   952→- **`pwdfun`{: #option-pwdfun } with `t:pwdfun_4/0`** - Provides a function for\n   953→  password validation. This could used for calling an external system or\n   954→  handling passwords stored as hash values.\n   955→\n   956→  This fun can also be used to make delays in authentication tries for example\n   957→  by calling `timer:sleep/1`.\n   958→\n   959→  To facilitate for instance counting of failed tries, the `State` variable\n   960→  could be used. This state is per connection only. The first time the pwdfun is\n   961→  called for a connection, the `State` variable has the value `undefined`.\n   962→\n   963→  The fun should return:\n   964→\n   965→  - `true` if the user and password is valid\n   966→  - `false` if the user or password is invalid\n   967→  - `disconnect` if a SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT message should be sent immediately. It\n   968→    will be followed by a close of the underlying tcp connection.\n   969→  - `{true, NewState:any()}` if the user and password is valid\n   970→  - `{false, NewState:any()}` if the user or password is invalid\n   971→\n   972→  A third usage is to block login attempts from a missbehaving peer. The `State`\n   973→  described above can be used for this. The return value `disconnect` is useful\n   974→  for this.\n   975→\n   976→  In case of the [`pk_check_user`](`m:ssh#option-pk_check_user`) is set, the\n   977→  atom `pubkey` is put in the password argument when validating a public key\n   978→  login. The pwdfun is then responsible to check that the user name is valid.\n   979→\n   980→- **`pwdfun` with `t:pwdfun_2/0`** - Provides a function for password\n   981→  validation. This function is called with user and password as strings, and\n   982→  returns:\n   983→\n   984→  - `true` if the user and password is valid\n   985→  - `false` if the user or password is invalid\n   986→\n   987→  In case of the [`pk_check_user`](`m:ssh#option-pk_check_user`) is set, the\n   988→  atom `pubkey` is put in the password argument when validating a public key\n   989→  login. The pwdfun is then responsible to check that the user name is valid.\n   990→\n   991→  This variant is kept for compatibility.\n   992→\n   993→- **`no_auth_needed`{: #option-no_auth_needed }** - If `true`, a client is\n   994→  authenticated without any need of providing any password or key.\n   995→\n   996→  This option is only intended for very special applications due to the high\n   997→  risk of accepting any connecting client.\n   998→\n   999→  The default value is `false`.\n  1000→\"\"\".\n  1001→-doc(#{title => <<\"Daemon Options\">>}).\n  1002→-type pwdfun_4() :: fun((User::string(),\n  1003→                         Password::string()|pubkey,\n  1004→                         PeerAddress::ip_port(),\n  1005→                         State::any()) ->\n  1006→                               boolean() | disconnect | {boolean(),NewState::any()}\n  1007→                       ) .\n  1008→\n  1009→-doc(#{title => <<\"Daemon Options\">>}).\n  1010→-type diffie_hellman_group_exchange_daemon_option() ::\n  1011→        {dh_gex_groups, [explicit_group()] | explicit_group_file() | ssh_moduli_file()}\n  1012→      | {dh_gex_limits, {Min::pos_integer(), Max::pos_integer()} } .\n  1013→\n  1014→-doc(#{title => <<\"Daemon Options\">>}).\n  1015→-type explicit_group() :: {Size::pos_integer(),G::pos_integer(),P::pos_integer()} .\n  1016→-doc(#{title => <<\"Daemon Options\">>}).\n  1017→-type explicit_group_file() :: {file,string()} .\n  1018→-doc \"\"\"\n  1019→- **`dh_gex_groups`** - Defines the groups the server may choose among when\n  1020→  diffie-hellman-group-exchange is negotiated. Understanding these patterns is critical for fixing authentication vulnerabilities.\n\n## Pattern Matching Basics\n\n### Records in Pattern Matching\n\n```erlang\n% Match and extract fields\nprocess(#ssh{authenticated = true, user = User}) ->\n    io:format(\"Authenticated user: ~p~n\", [User])\n\n% Match specific field value\nprocess(#ssh{authenticated = false}) ->\n    error(\"Not authenticated\")\n\n% Ignore unwanted fields with underscore\nprocess(#ssh{authenticated = Auth, _other = _}) ->\n    case Auth of\n        true -> allow_operation();\n        false -> deny_operation()\n    end\n```\n\n### Multiple Clauses\n\nErlang evaluates clauses top-to-bottom, so order matters:\n\n```erlang\n% Specific clause (more restrictive)\nhandle_msg(Msg, _Data, _Role, SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    process_authenticated(Msg);\n\n% General clause (less restrictive) - catches everything else\nhandle_msg(_Msg, _Data, _Role, _SSH) ->\n    send_error(\"Not authenticated\").\n```\n\n## Guard Clauses\n\nGuard clauses restrict when a function clause matches. They come after `when`:\n\n```erlang\nfunction(Arg) when Arg > 5 ->\n    % Only matches if Arg is > 5\n    io:format(\"Large: ~p~n\", [Arg]);\n\nfunction(Arg) ->\n    % Matches anything else\n    io:format(\"Small: ~p~n\", [Arg]).\n```\n\n### Record Guards\n\nFor records, you can guard on field values:\n\n```erlang\nhandle_message(Msg, SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    % Only if authenticated field is true\n    process_secure_message(Msg);\n\nhandle_message(_Msg, _SSH) ->\n    % Handles all non-authenticated cases\n    send_error(\"Authentication required\").\n```\n\n### Multiple Conditions in Guards\n\nUse commas (logical AND) or semicolons (logical OR):\n\n```erlang\n% AND conditions (all must be true)\nprocess(SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated, SSH#ssh.role =:= server ->\n    allow_server_operation();\n\n% OR conditions (any can be true)\nprocess(SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated; SSH#ssh.trusted ->\n    allow_operation().\n```\n\n## Common Guard Functions\n\n```erlang\n% Arithmetic comparisons\nX > Y, X < Y, X >= Y, X =< Y, X =:= Y, X =/= Y\n\n% Type checking\nis_atom(X), is_number(X), is_list(X), is_tuple(X), is_pid(X)\n\n% List operations\nlength(List) > 5\n\n% Boolean\nis_boolean(X), X =:= true, X =:= false\n```\n\n## Refactoring Vulnerable Code\n\n### Before: Ignoring Authentication\n\n```erlang\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{channel_type = Type},\n           Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    % VULNERABLE: _SSH parameter is ignored\n    setup_channel(Connection, Type).\n```\n\n### After: Checking Authentication\n\n```erlang\n% Specific clause for authenticated connections\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{channel_type = Type},\n           Connection, server, SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    setup_channel(Connection, Type);\n\n% Catch-all clause for unauthenticated connections\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{},\n           _Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    send_error(\"Not authenticated\").\n```\n\n## Best Practices\n\n### 1. Never Ignore Security-Critical Parameters\n\n**Bad:**\n```erlang\nhandler(Data, _SSH) ->  % Underscore means \"I'm ignoring this\"\n    process(Data)\n```\n\n**Good:**\n```erlang\nhandler(Data, SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    process(Data);\nhandler(_Data, _SSH) ->\n    deny_access()\n```\n\n### 2. Order Clauses from Specific to General\n\n```erlang\n% DO: Specific conditions first\noperation(SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated, SSH#ssh.role =:= server ->\n    allow();\n\noperation(SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    restricted_allow();\n\noperation(_SSH) ->\n    deny().\n\n% DON'T: General conditions first (specific clauses unreachable)\noperation(_SSH) ->\n    allow();  % This matches everything, nothing else runs!\n\noperation(SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    deny();  % This never executes\n```\n\n### 3. Use Explicit Guards for Security\n\n```erlang\n% Clear and explicit\nhandler(Msg, Connection, server, SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated =:= true ->\n    process(Msg);\n\nhandler(_Msg, _Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    send_error(\"Not authenticated\").\n```\n\n## Erlang Pattern Syntax Reference\n\n### Record Patterns\n\n```erlang\n% Full pattern\n#record_name{field1 = Value1, field2 = Value2}\n\n% Partial pattern (other fields ignored)\n#record_name{field1 = Value1}\n\n% With underscore (field name but ignore value)\n#record_name{field1 = _Value1}\n\n% Pattern with condition in guard\n#record_name{authenticated = Auth} when Auth =:= true\n```\n\n### Common Security Patterns\n\n```erlang\n% Only authenticated users\nauth_required(SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    allow();\nauth_required(_) ->\n    deny().\n\n% Server-side authenticated operations\nserver_operation(Msg, SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated, SSH#ssh.role =:= server ->\n    execute(Msg);\nserver_operation(_, _) ->\n    deny().\n\n% Multiple checks\nsecure_op(SSH) when\n    SSH#ssh.authenticated =:= true,\n    SSH#ssh.role =:= server,\n    SSH#ssh.user =/= anonymous ->\n    execute();\nsecure_op(_) ->\n    deny().\n```\n\n## When Guards Fail\n\nCommon mistakes:\n\n```erlang\n% WRONG: Guard function doesn't exist\nbad(X) when my_custom_check(X) ->  % Compile error if my_custom_check/1 doesn't exist\n    ok.\n\n% WRONG: Trying to call non-deterministic functions in guards\nbad(X) when random:uniform() > 0.5 ->  % Compile error\n    ok.\n\n% RIGHT: Use only built-in guard functions or simple comparisons\ngood(X) when X > 5, X < 10 ->\n    ok.\n```\n\n## Testing Guard Effectiveness\n\nWrite test cases for all clause paths:\n\n```erlang\ntest_authenticated_allowed() ->\n    SSH = #ssh{authenticated = true, role = server},\n    {allowed, _} = handle_msg(msg, conn, server, SSH).\n\ntest_unauthenticated_denied() ->\n    SSH = #ssh{authenticated = false, role = server},\n    {error, _} = handle_msg(msg, conn, server, SSH).\n\ntest_wrong_role_denied() ->\n    SSH = #ssh{authenticated = true, role = client},\n    {error, _} = handle_msg(msg, conn, server, SSH).\n```\n\n## References\n\n- Erlang Documentation: Pattern Matching and Guards\n- Erlang Specification: Guards and Guard Sequences\n- SSH Authentication Understanding these message types is critical for identifying and fixing vulnerability windows where unauthenticated clients can send privileged messages.\n\n## SSH Message Type Categories\n\n### Transport Layer Messages (RFC 4253)\n\nThese messages are for key exchange and algorithm negotiation. They should be allowed before authentication.\n\n- **SSH_MSG_KEXINIT** (20): Key exchange algorithm negotiation\n- **SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS** (21): Marks start of encrypted traffic\n- **SSH_MSG_SERVICE_REQUEST** (5): Request a service (ssh-userauth, ssh-connection)\n- **SSH_MSG_SERVICE_ACCEPT** (6): Service accepted\n\n### User Authentication Messages (RFC 4252)\n\nThese messages are for the authentication phase:\n\n- **SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST** (50): Client sends credentials\n- **SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_SUCCESS** (52): Authentication succeeded\n- **SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_FAILURE** (51): Authentication failed\n- **SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_BANNER** (53): Server sends banner\n\n### Connection Protocol Messages (RFC 4254)\n\nThese messages are for channel operations and should ONLY be allowed AFTER successful authentication:\n\n```erlang\n% In ssh_connect.hrl:\n-define(SSH_MSG_GLOBAL_REQUEST,         80).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN,           90).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN_CONFIRMATION, 91).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN_FAILURE,   92).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_DATA,           94).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_EXTENDED_DATA,  95).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_EOF,            96).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_CLOSE,          97).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST,        98).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_SUCCESS,        99).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_FAILURE,        100).\n```\n\n**Critical Messages for Command Execution:**\n\n- **SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN** (90): Opens a \"session\" channel - VULNERABLE\n- **SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST** (98): Sends requests like \"exec\", \"shell\" - VULNERABLE\n\n## RFC 4254 Channel Types\n\nWhen SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN is received:\n\n```\nstring    channel type in US-ASCII only\nuint32    sender's initial window size\nuint32    sender's maximum packet size\n.... channel type specific data follows\n```\n\nDangerous channel types:\n\n- **\"session\"** - Opens a shell/exec channel - VULNERABLE\n- **\"direct-tcpip\"** - Port forwarding - VULNERABLE if allowed\n- **\"forwarded-tcpip\"** - Remote port forwarding\n\n## RFC 4254 Channel Request Types\n\nWhen SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST is received on a session channel:\n\n```\nstring    request type in US-ASCII\nboolean   want reply\n.... request type specific data\n```\n\nDangerous request types:\n\n- **\"exec\"** - Execute command - VULNERABLE\n  - Data: `string command`\n  - Allows direct command execution\n\n- **\"shell\"** - Start shell - VULNERABLE\n  - No additional data\n  - Starts interactive shell\n\n- **\"subsystem\"** - Execute subsystem (e.g., SFTP) - VULNERABLE\n  - Data: `string subsystem name`\n  - Runs predefined subsystems\n\n- **\"env\"** - Set environment variables - VULNERABLE\n  - Data: `string variable name`, `string variable value`\n  - Sets environment before command execution\n\n- **\"pty-req\"** - Allocate pseudo-terminal - POTENTIALLY VULNERABLE\n  - Data: terminal type, dimensions, etc.\n\n## State Machine and Message Acceptance\n\n### Pre-Authentication States\n\nIn these states, ONLY transport and auth messages should be processed:\n\n```\nkexinit -> key_exchange -> userauth\n```\n\n**Allowed:**\n- SSH_MSG_KEXINIT\n- SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS\n- SSH_MSG_SERVICE_REQUEST\n- SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_*\n\n**BLOCKED:**\n- SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN\n- SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST\n- SSH_MSG_GLOBAL_REQUEST\n\n### Post-Authentication State\n\nAfter transitioning to `connected`:\n\n```\nconnected\n```\n\n**Allowed:**\n- All connection protocol messages\n- Channel operations\n- Global requests\n\n### The Vulnerability Window\n\nThe vulnerability exists when:\n\n1. Client reaches `connected` state without authentication\n2. Server processes SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN without checking `authenticated`\n3. Server processes SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST without checking `authenticated`\n\nThis allows:\n\n```\nUnauthenticated Client → SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN (session)\n                      → SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST (exec, \"id\")\n                      → Command executes!\n```\n\n## Message Encoding/Decoding\n\nIn Erlang, messages are encoded/decoded using binary patterns:\n\n### SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN Encoding\n\n```erlang\n#ssh_msg_channel_open{\n    channel_type = \"session\",\n    sender_channel = 0,\n    initial_window_size = 32768,\n    maximum_packet_size = 32768\n}\n```\n\nBinary format:\n```\nByte     Type Name         Value\n1        byte             90 (SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN)\n5-8      uint32           sender_channel\n9-12     uint32           initial_window_size\n13-16    uint32           maximum_packet_size\n17-20    uint32           length of channel type\n21-...   string           channel type (\"session\")\n```\n\n### SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST Encoding\n\n```erlang\n#ssh_msg_channel_request{\n    recipient_channel = ChannelId,\n    request_type = \"exec\",\n    want_reply = true,\n    data = <<\"id\">>\n}\n```\n\nBinary format:\n```\nByte     Type Name           Value\n1        byte               98 (SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST)\n2-5      uint32             recipient_channel\n6-9      uint32             length of request type\n10-...   string             request type (\"exec\")\n...+1    boolean            want_reply\n...+5    uint32             length of command\n...+...  string             command (\"id\")\n```\n\n## Detecting the Vulnerability\n\nLook for these patterns in the source code:\n\n### Pattern 1: Processing Channel Messages Without Auth Check\n\n```erlang\n% In ssh_connection.erl\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{...},\n           Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    % VULNERABLE: _SSH is ignored\n    setup_channel(Connection, ...)\n```\n\n### Pattern 2: Connection Message Handler Without Guards\n\n```erlang\n% In ssh_connection_handler.erl\nhandle_event(internal, {conn_msg, Msg}, StateName, Data) ->\n    % VULNERABLE: No check that Data#data.ssh_params#ssh.authenticated\n    ssh_connection:handle_msg(Msg, ...)\n```\n\n### Pattern 3: Role Check Without Auth Check\n\n```erlang\nhandle_msg(Msg, Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    % VULNERABLE: Checks role but not authentication\n    process_server_message(Msg)\n```\n\n## The Fix\n\nAdd authentication checks before processing channel messages:\n\n```erlang\n% SECURE: Only authenticated users\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{...} = Msg,\n           Connection, server, SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    setup_channel(Connection, Msg);\n\n% SECURE: Reject unauthenticated attempts\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{recipient_channel = ChannelId},\n           Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    send_channel_open_failure(Connection, ChannelId, ...);\n\n% SECURE: Only authenticated users\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_request{...} = Msg,\n           Connection, server, SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    process_request(Connection, Msg);\n\n% SECURE: Reject unauthenticated attempts\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_request{recipient_channel = ChannelId},\n           Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    send_channel_failure(Connection, ChannelId)\n```\n\n## References\n\n- RFC 4254: The Secure Shell (SSH) Connection Protocol\n- RFC 4252: The Secure Shell (SSH) Authentication Protocol\n- Erlang SSH source: `ssh_connect.hrl` (message They should be allowed before authentication.\n\n- **SSH_MSG_KEXINIT** (20): Key exchange algorithm negotiation\n- **SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS** (21): Marks start of encrypted traffic\n- **SSH_MSG_SERVICE_REQUEST** (5): Request a service (ssh-userauth, ssh-connection)\n- **SSH_MSG_SERVICE_ACCEPT** (6): Service accepted\n\n### User Authentication Messages (RFC 4252)\n\nThese messages are for the authentication phase:\n\n- **SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST** (50): Client sends credentials\n- **SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_SUCCESS** (52): Authentication succeeded\n- **SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_FAILURE** (51): Authentication failed\n- **SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_BANNER** (53): Server sends banner\n\n### Connection Protocol Messages (RFC 4254)\n\nThese messages are for channel operations and should ONLY be allowed AFTER successful authentication:\n\n```erlang\n% In ssh_connect.hrl:\n-define(SSH_MSG_GLOBAL_REQUEST,         80).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN,           90).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN_CONFIRMATION, 91).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN_FAILURE,   92).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_DATA,           94).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_EXTENDED_DATA,  95).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_EOF,            96).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_CLOSE,          97).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST,        98).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_SUCCESS,        99).\n-define(SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_FAILURE,        100).\n```\n\n**Critical Messages for Command Execution:**\n\n- **SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN** (90): Opens a \"session\" channel - VULNERABLE\n- **SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST** (98): Sends requests like \"exec\", \"shell\" - VULNERABLE\n\n## RFC 4254 Channel Types\n\nWhen SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN is received:\n\n```\nstring    channel type in US-ASCII only\nuint32    sender's initial window size\nuint32    sender's maximum packet size\n.... channel type specific data follows\n```\n\nDangerous channel types:\n\n- **\"session\"** - Opens a shell/exec channel - VULNERABLE\n- **\"direct-tcpip\"** - Port forwarding - VULNERABLE if allowed\n- **\"forwarded-tcpip\"** - Remote port forwarding\n\n## RFC 4254 Channel Request Types\n\nWhen SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST is received on a session channel:\n\n```\nstring    request type in US-ASCII\nboolean   want reply\n.... request type specific data\n```\n\nDangerous request types:\n\n- **\"exec\"** - Execute command - VULNERABLE\n  - Data: `string command`\n  - Allows direct command execution\n\n- **\"shell\"** - Start shell - VULNERABLE\n  - No additional data\n  - Starts interactive shell\n\n- **\"subsystem\"** - Execute subsystem (e.g., SFTP) - VULNERABLE\n  - Data: `string subsystem name`\n  - Runs predefined subsystems\n\n- **\"env\"** - Set environment variables - VULNERABLE\n  - Data: `string variable name`, `string variable value`\n  - Sets environment before command execution\n\n- **\"pty-req\"** - Allocate pseudo-terminal - POTENTIALLY VULNERABLE\n  - Data: terminal type, dimensions, etc.\n\n## State Machine and Message Acceptance\n\n### Pre-Authentication States\n\nIn these states, ONLY transport and auth messages should be processed:\n\n```\nkexinit -> key_exchange -> userauth\n```\n\n**Allowed:**\n- SSH_MSG_KEXINIT\n- SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS\n- SSH_MSG_SERVICE_REQUEST\n- SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_*\n\n**BLOCKED:**\n- SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN\n- SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST\n- SSH_MSG_GLOBAL_REQUEST\n\n### Post-Authentication State\n\nAfter transitioning to `connected`:\n\n```\nconnected\n```\n\n**Allowed:**\n- All connection protocol messages\n- Channel operations\n- Global requests\n\n### The Vulnerability Window\n\nThe vulnerability exists when:\n\n1. Client reaches `connected` state without authentication\n2. Server processes SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN without checking `authenticated`\n3. Server processes SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST without checking `authenticated`\n\nThis allows:\n\n```\nUnauthenticated Client → SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN (session)\n                      → SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST (exec, \"id\")\n                      → Command executes!\n```\n\n## Message Encoding/Decoding\n\nIn Erlang, messages are encoded/decoded using binary patterns:\n\n### SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN Encoding\n\n```erlang\n#ssh_msg_channel_open{\n    channel_type = \"session\",\n    sender_channel = 0,\n    initial_window_size = 32768,\n    maximum_packet_size = 32768\n}\n```\n\nBinary format:\n```\nByte     Type Name         Value\n1        byte             90 (SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN)\n5-8      uint32           sender_channel\n9-12     uint32           initial_window_size\n13-16    uint32           maximum_packet_size\n17-20    uint32           length of channel type\n21-...   string           channel type (\"session\")\n```\n\n### SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST Encoding\n\n```erlang\n#ssh_msg_channel_request{\n    recipient_channel = ChannelId,\n    request_type = \"exec\",\n    want_reply = true,\n    data = <<\"id\">>\n}\n```\n\nBinary format:\n```\nByte     Type Name           Value\n1        byte               98 (SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST)\n2-5      uint32             recipient_channel\n6-9      uint32             length of request type\n10-...   string             request type (\"exec\")\n...+1    boolean            want_reply\n...+5    uint32             length of command\n...+...  string             command (\"id\")\n```\n\n## Detecting the Vulnerability\n\nLook for these patterns in the source code:\n\n### Pattern 1: Processing Channel Messages Without Auth Check\n\n```erlang\n% In ssh_connection.erl\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{...},\n           Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    % VULNERABLE: _SSH is ignored\n    setup_channel(Connection, ...)\n```\n\n### Pattern 2: Connection Message Handler Without Guards\n\n```erlang\n% In ssh_connection_handler.erl\nhandle_event(internal, {conn_msg, Msg}, StateName, Data) ->\n    % VULNERABLE: No check that Data#data.ssh_params#ssh.authenticated\n    ssh_connection:handle_msg(Msg, ...)\n```\n\n### Pattern 3: Role Check Without Auth Check\n\n```erlang\nhandle_msg(Msg, Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    % VULNERABLE: Checks role but not authentication\n    process_server_message(Msg)\n```\n\n## The Fix\n\nAdd authentication checks before processing channel messages:\n\n```erlang\n% SECURE: Only authenticated users\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{...} = Msg,\n           Connection, server, SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    setup_channel(Connection, Msg);\n\n% SECURE: Reject unauthenticated attempts\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{recipient_channel = ChannelId},\n           Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    send_channel_open_failure(Connection, ChannelId, ...);\n\n% SECURE: Only authenticated users\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_request{...} = Msg,\n           Connection, server, SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    process_request(Connection, Msg);\n\n% SECURE: Reject unauthenticated attempts\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_request{recipient_channel = ChannelId},\n           Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    send_channel_failure(Connection, ChannelId)\n```\n\n## References\n\n- RFC 4254: The Secure Shell (SSH) Connection Protocol\n- RFC 4252: The Secure Shell (SSH) Authentication Protocol\n- Erlang SSH source: `ssh_connect.hrl` (message constants)\n- Erlang SSH source: `ssh_connection.erl` (message handlers)\n","structuredPatch":[],"originalFile":null}}

  %% This daemon instance has not enabled tcpip_forwarding\n            {[{connection_reply, request_failure_msg()}], Connection};\n\n        true ->\n            ConnectionSup = The authentication status was available in the `SSH` record's `authenticated` field but was systematically ignored in critical message handlers.\n\n### Key Issues:\n\n1. **Ignored Parameter**: Handler functions had a parameter `_SSH` (with underscore prefix) indicating the parameter was intentionally ignored\n2. **Missing Guard Clauses**: No Erlang guard clauses checking `SSH#ssh.authenticated`\n3. **No Catch-All Rejection**: No fallback clauses to reject unauthenticated requests\n\n## Affected Message Types\n\nThe following SSH message types could be exploited without authentication:\n\n### 1. SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN (type 90)\n- **\"session\"** channel type - Opens shell/exec channel\n- **\"direct-tcpip\"** channel type - Port forwarding\n\n### 2. SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST (type 98)\n- **\"exec\"** - Execute arbitrary commands\n- **\"shell\"** - Start interactive shell\n- **\"subsystem\"** - Run subsystems (e.g., SFTP)\n- **\"env\"** - Set environment variables before execution\n\n### 3. SSH_MSG_GLOBAL_REQUEST (type 80)\n- **\"tcpip-forward\"** - Setup remote port forwarding\n\n## Attack Flow\n\n```\nUnauthenticated SSH Client\n    ↓\nComplete Key Exchange (allowed before auth)\n    ↓\nSend SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN with \"session\" (VULNERABLE)\n    ↓\nSend SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST \"exec\" (VULNERABLE)\n    ↓\nCommand Executes on Server (as authenticated user context)\n    ↓\nAttacker receives output\n```\n\n## Files Modified\n\n**File**: `/app/workspace/otp_src_27.3.2/lib/ssh/src/ssh_connection.erl`\n\n## Security Fixes Applied\n\n### Fix Pattern\n\nFor each vulnerable message handler, applied the following pattern:\n\n```erlang\n%% BEFORE (VULNERABLE):\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{...}, Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    % Processes request without checking authentication\n    setup_channel(Connection, ...);\n\n%% AFTER (SECURE):\n% Authenticated path - only processes if authenticated\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{...}, Connection, server, SSH)\n    when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    setup_channel(Connection, ...);\n\n% Unauthenticated path - rejects request\nhandle_msg(#ssh_msg_channel_open{...}, Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    send_failure(Connection, \"Unauthorized\");\n```\n\n### Specific Fixes\n\n#### 1. conditions before the function clause matches:\n\n```erlang\n% This clause ONLY matches if SSH#ssh.authenticated evaluates to true\nhandle_msg(Msg, Connection, server, SSH) when SSH#ssh.authenticated ->\n    allow_operation(Msg)\n\n% This clause matches everything else (not authenticated)\nhandle_msg(Msg, Connection, server, _SSH) ->\n    deny_operation(Msg)\n```\n\nGuards are evaluated at pattern-match time, making them efficient and preventing any possibility of skipping the check.\n\n### Catch-All Rejection Pattern\n\nEach vulnerable message type now has TWO clauses:\n\n1. **Authenticated Clause**: Processes the request (same logic as before)\n2. **Unauthenticated Clause**: Rejects with appropriate error message\n\nErlang evaluates clauses top-to-bottom, so:\n- Authenticated requests match the first clause and are processed\n- Unauthenticated requests fail the guard and fall through to the rejection clause\n\n## Verification\n\nAll 7 vulnerable message types now have:\n- ✅ Guard clause checking `SSH#ssh.authenticated`\n- ✅ Explicit rejection clause for unauthenticated attempts\n- ✅ Appropriate error messages (SSH_OPEN_ADMINISTRATIVELY_PROHIBITED or SSH_MSG_GLOBAL_REQUEST | \"tcpip-forward\" | 1276-1309 | MEDIUM |\n\n## Security Fixes Applied\n\n### Fix Strategy\n\nTwo-part approach for each vulnerable handler:\n\n1. **Add Authentication Guard
